newsitem.title: USA: Divided commission releases Social Security report.
newsitem.headline: Divided commission releases Social Security report.

text.p: A divided advisory panel Monday issued conflicting plans for ensuring Social Security's long-term solvency but agreed some of the program's hefty payroll taxes should be invested in financial markets.
The 13-member advisory group was appointed in 1994 to devise ways to guarantee the future health of Social Security, which provides retirement and other aid to 44 million Americans.

The council split into three factions, coming together on smaller but important provisions but never agreeing on an overall plan. Without change, the Social Security trust fund will be depleted in 2030 as baby-boomers retire.

Despite the lack of consensus, Health Secretary Donna Shalala and Social Security Commissioner Shirley Chater issued a joint statement saying, "Let there be no doubt. Social Security will be there for generations to come."

One five-member faction of the council called for radical privatisation that would turn Social Security into a two-tiered benefit system. Under this plan all retirees would get a basic, flat benefit of about half what they get now and individuals would set up personal savings accounts, similar to individual retirement accounts (IRAs), and make investment decisions.

Five percentage points of the annual Social Security payroll tax would be re-directed to these accounts. The actual benefit from the account would vary from person to person, depending on the success of an individual's investments.
The transition to the new system would be financed by a tax equal to 1.5 percent of payroll.

"(This) plan holds the promise of larger and more secure retirement incomes for workers. It also holds real promise for boosting national saving," said Carloyn Weaver of the American Enterprise Institute, a commission member who backs it.
A similar plan, supported by part of the council, would add individual investment accounts to the system, financed by a new, mandatory contribution of 1.6 percent of payroll.

A third, six-member group, including labour union officials and former Social Security Commissioner Robert Ball, wants to preserve much of the current benefits structure but says the government should study investing around 40 percent of the Social Security trust fund in stocks and bonds.

Currently, Social Security funds can be invested only in Treasury securities, which provide a lower rate of return than the private market. Estimates are that shifting into market-based funds could increase the program's rate of return to 4.2 percent from the current 2.3 percent.
Ball said he would support changing the government investment mix now but his allies want to study this first.

At a news conference Monday, labour representatives pledged an all-out fight to block any move in Congres toward individual investment accounts, charging they would devastate the system and result in higher Social Security taxes and lower benefits for many retirees.

"The more radical of the proposals to dismantle Social Security would basically make the securities industry reponsible for administering America's basic retirement security," Ball said. "There is simply no compelling argument for abandoning the traditional Social Security programme."
The financial industry has started lobbying Congress in favour of privatisation.
Some lawmakers found words of encouragement in the divided council's report.

"For the first time ever, all members of a Social Security advisory council ... have recommended that some of Social Security's funds be invested in the private marketplace," Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth said. "That greatly increases the chance that Congress will adopt some kind of investment option," the Delaware Republican added.

Senate Democratic Leader Thomas Daschle backs the idea of the government investing some trust funds in private markets, while Nebraska Democratic Sen Robert Kerrey wants to divert a tenth of the 12.4 percent Social Security payroll tax to $1,000 savings accounts for every U.S. baby.
The American Association of Retired Persons, the nation's largest senior citizen's group, denounced plans for individual accounts, saying "there is no need to rush to radical reform."

Overall, the council agreed on changes that would solve a large chunk of the Social Security financing problem. Those include extending Social Security to new state and local govenrment employees and requiring retirees to pay taxes on benefits that exceed what they paid into the system.
Social Security income, taxes plus interest on the trust fund will exceed expenses until 2020. By 2030, without changes the system will no longer be able to pay full benefits.
